rv.q: “The Shark Is Broken” is not a play for the ages, or even for those who have never seen “Jaws,” but it’s a frisky and continuously amusing diversion—perfect late-summer entertainment if you want to stay away from the ocean.
Were it not for its curious meta-story, the play would be little more than a pleasant diversion: 95 minutes of bloodless, toothless, Hollywood-adjacent dramedy.
Copying has its costs; certain kinds of reverence are corrosive.
Intense and lean, it handily outmatches the preceding scenes of uneasy boatmates bobbing in the drink.
On Broadway, it feels a bit out of its depth.
That extra-textural dramatic irony gnaws at The Shark Is Broken, which has less integrity as a play than as a thoroughly researched dress-up presentation for a history-of-film class.
Still, on Broadway, the little play gets swallowed up like a doomed teen in Amity.
Shaw and Nixon set out to depict the monotony of movie sets, where actors can wait for hours between takes, and in the process they put their audience to sleep — literally.

But it makes for thin Broadway gruel, alas, with a 90-minute running time, a straight-up POV, and a series of behind-the-camera recreations of a situation that already has been much dissected and discussed.
Ian Shaw has co-written a clever, generous play with three terrific performances.
Fortunately, this one did not jump the shark.
The Shark Is Broken is a delightful backstage comedy that captures the frustration and camaraderie of three men stuck on a boat during the famously troubled filming of Jaws.
Happily, they all succeed in spades.
Whatever he’s doing, its mighty funny.
As it bites into movie history, The Shark Is Broken makes for a diversion worth sea-ing.
Admittedly, if someone else were portraying Robert, without all of the meta undercurrents, it’s unlikely The Shark Is Broken would be as touching.
And while for the characters themselves, being stuck on the boat is presented as some form of intolerable torture — for audiences, it's definitely a wild ride worth taking.
With spot-on comedic timing, these three are the reason the show works at all.

The Shark is Broken, [is] an amiable, funny, beautifully acted piece that remains in dramatic dry dock all night long… watching these three shoot the breeze may leave you hungry for a little action, especially when the dialogue is so weighed down with dramatic irony jokes.

But, like the shark itself, the play’s essential functions scarcely work — save for the few scenes in which the three men, caught in an epochal shift in acting and celebrity, wax poetic about the fall of fathers, the impotence of sons, and the rolling tides of art.
But it is also a slow and static piece built around a premise that probably could not sustain much more than a five-minute “Saturday Night Live” sketch.
Back to the Future is easy, familiar fun and by the end of the evening, I was rooting for Marty and his family, even as I was aware of the show’s shortcomings.
But what most made me critically seasick in The Shark Is Broken was the bombast of its acting, especially the excessively shouting Shaw and the frenetically paranoid Brightman.
On Broadway, it feels a little like one more example of the thing it claims to be critiquing.
The production is not an embarrassment.
I hate to carp, but while Jaws may be the ultimate fish story, The Shark Is Broken flounders to the end, with neither an engaging hook nor a line of compelling dialog to keep it afloat.
Ian Shaw imitates his father’s every grimace and vocal mannerism, delivering one of the most grating performances ever put on stage.
The Shark Is Broken is a sensational night at the theater, especially if you're a Jaws fan.
A "Jaws" aficionado will appreciate this one
“The Shark is Broken” gives us a look behind the scenes of an iconic film and sometimes the background is even more interesting than the film itself.
The Shark is Broken simply wasn’t a comedy, and even those among the audience who would have enjoyed this kind of character study were primed for a different experience.

While the sea and the circumstances provide plenty of drama, Nixon and Shaw’s script fails to dig much beyond intel widely available through previously produced documentaries, including Inside Jaws and The Shark is Still Working.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this behind-the-scenes comedy about the troubled "Jaws" shoot, with some praising the performances and nostalgic appeal while others find it dramatically inert and overly reliant on fan knowledge.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.

vr.q: Ultimately, I found this show really, really compelling, but it's definitely not going to be for everyone.
So yeah overall I think it is a really great production of a play that just didn't resonate with me. But I definitely don't think that means that it won't resonate with you.
